parsed.summary: The Lean file states that for every Dirichlet character χ modulo q ≥ 1 and every complex s with Re s > 7/8, other than the pair (χ trivial, s = 1), Mathlib's Dirichlet L-function L(s,χ) is nonzero. This matches the Dirichlet-character part of the paper's main theorem, including ζ at q = 1. The main caveat is that the Hecke L-function part over Q(√-3) is not formalized.

glossary.plain: The meromorphic/entire continuation of L(s,χ) = Σ χ(n) n^{-s}, with χ extended by zero on non-units. For the trivial character it is ζ(s)·∏_{p|q}(1-p^{-s}), with a junk value at s = 1.
glossary.note: For χ ≠ 1 it is entire. For χ = 1 the only pole is at s = 1, and hpole excludes that point. The imprimitive Euler factors ∏_{p|q}(1-p^{-s}) have no zeros for Re s > 0.

glossary.plain: For q ≠ 0, χ a Dirichlet character mod q over ℂ, and Re s > 7/8 with not (χ = 1 and s = 1), L(s,χ) ≠ 0.
glossary.standard_concept: No zeros of Dirichlet L-functions in Re s > 7/8
glossary.note: χ = 1 is the principal character mod q. The hypothesis [NeZero q] just means a modulus q ≥ 1.

lean_claims.plain: For every q ≥ 1, every Dirichlet character χ mod q, and every s ∈ ℂ with Re s > 7/8 and (χ, s) ≠ (trivial, 1), the Mathlib L-function value LFunction χ s is nonzero.

paper_claims.plain: Every finite-order Hecke L-function over Q(√-3) has no zero in Re s > 7/8.
Every Dirichlet L-function, including ζ, has no zero in Re s > 7/8. A pole at s = 1 for a principal character is allowed.

coverage.why: The Lean statement is the zero-free claim over all moduli q ≥ 1, with the pole point s = 1 for the trivial character excluded. Mathlib's L-function agrees with the L-series on Re s > 1 and with the continuation elsewhere.
No Hecke characters or Hecke L-functions over Q(√-3) appear in the Lean file.

flags.explanation: The paper's main theorem has two parts, Hecke L-functions over Q(√-3) and Dirichlet L-functions. Only the Dirichlet part is formalized, so the Lean theorem does not cover the headline Hecke claim.

LFunction 1 1 takes a convention value at the pole. hpole excludes exactly this case, matching the paper's 'a pole at s = 1 is allowed'. Because χ ≠ 1 gives an entire function and χ = 1 has its only pole at s = 1, no other pole is hit.
flags.probe_idea: Check that for χ ≠ 1 the Mathlib LFunction is differentiable, e.g. via DirichletCharacter.differentiable_LFunction.

lint_verdicts.why: (7/8 : ℝ) is a real literal division, which is exactly 0.875, so there is no truncation.
The only pole of the L-function is at s = 1 for the trivial character, and hpole excludes it.
The conclusion LFunction χ s ≠ 0 is never evaluated at the convention-valued pole, because hpole excludes (χ = 1, s = 1).
